item.title: 'Stunning' Percolation Proof Solves Decades-Old Puzzle About Phase Transitions
item.description: Problem. Past a critical threshold, isolated clusters must snap into one connected mass — proven for grid lattices, never for every infinite network. Approach. Five ETH Zurich mathematicians assumed a cluster survived past the threshold, then studied its boundary ("shoreline"). A boundary that long can't stay sealed off — it must connect outward. They ran a technique called sprinkling in reverse, simplifying the proof for any uniform network. Result. Supercritical sharpness now holds for all infinite transitive graphs — the first fully general proof. Why it matters. Percolation is the simplest model of phase transitions, which also govern epidemics and wildfires. Jargon: Percolation — connections spreading through a network. Phase transition — abrupt shift at a threshold. Critical probability — that threshold. Sprinkling — adding connections incrementally.

item.title: Faint far-infrared radiation drives a correlated insulator-to-metal transition in magic-angle graphene
item.description: Problem. Far-infrared light is hard to detect efficiently — sensors are bulky, slow, or need extreme cooling, limiting medical imaging and astronomy. Approach. Researchers stacked two graphene sheets at a "magic angle" (~1 degree), squeezing electrons into bands where they interact and freeze into an insulating state. Faint far-infrared light heats only the electrons, not the lattice, since the two barely exchange heat. Result. Even weak exposure heated electrons enough to melt the insulating state into a metal — a sensitive, voltage-tunable switch. Why it matters. A new detector platform for a wavelength that's historically hard to sense. Jargon: Magic-angle graphene — twisted layers with unusual electronics. Correlated insulator — non-conduction from electron interactions. Bolometer — detects radiation via heating. Far-infrared — long-wavelength light near microwave.
